strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The study evaluates 14 explanation methods across multiple model architectures (BERT, RoBERTa, LLaMA-3.2, Qwen-3), two hate speech benchmarks (Civil Comments, Jigsaw), and three demographic axes (race, gender, religion).

Nuanced and insightful findings: The paper draws a critical distinction between instance-level bias detection (RQ1, where explanations succeed) and cross-model selection (RQ2, where explanations fail), explaining that debiasing alters attribution landscapes across models and prevents direct calibration.

Meaningful methodological contributions to bias mitigation: By adopting a fairness-balanced tuning objective rather than purely task-performance tuning, the paper provides a well-justified counterpoint to prior pessimistic findings (e.g., Dimanov et al., 2020) regarding explanation-regularized debiasing.

Comparison with LLM-as-a-Judge and Faithfulness: The self-reflection/self-attribution comparison in Section 6 and the faithfulness decoupling analysis in Appendix G provide valuable practical insights for the XAI and algorithmic fairness communities.
Excellent clarity, reproducibility, and organization: The methodology, metrics, and experimental details are transparently reported, accompanied by extensive appendices covering full ablation setups.
weaknesses: Reliance on pre-defined sensitive token dictionaries: The operationalization of sensitive features relies on explicit identity-term lexicons and token-level substitutions. This setup struggles to capture subtle, intersectional, or implicit social biases where no explicit identity word is present.

Debiasing experiments restricted to encoder-only architectures: Due to the computational cost of differentiating through explanations, the debiasing regularization in RQ3 is evaluated only on encoder models (BERT, RoBERTa) and single bias types, leaving open how explanation-based regularization transfers to modern instruction-tuned decoder LLMs.

Counterfactual substitution validity: Generating counterfactual instances via exact keyword replacement can occasionally yield syntactically unnatural or out-of-distribution text, which may introduce minor artifacts into the individual unfairness calculations.

strengths: The paper presents a comprehensive and systematic empirical investigation bridging explainability and fairness, evaluating 14 explanation methods across multiple model architectures (both encoder-only models like BERT/RoBERTa and decoder-only LLMs like LLaMA-3.2 and Qwen3) and two benchmark datasets.

The evaluation is structured around clear and practically relevant research questions (bias detection, model selection, and bias mitigation), providing actionable and nuanced takeaways rather than oversimplified claims.

The paper directly addresses conflicting claims in prior literature regarding explanation faithfulness and adversarial concealment (e.g., Dimanov et al.), showing that L2- and Occlusion-based attributions remain robust indicators of bias even in debiased models when properly tuned.

The comparison between post-hoc feature attribution methods and LLM-as-a-judge approaches (self-reflection and self-attribution) is timely and provides valuable insights into the limitations of LLM self-critique for fairness.
The manuscript is well-written and structured, supported by extensive supplementary experiments and ablations covering fairness-utility trade-offs and explanation faithfulness.
weaknesses: The operationalization of bias relies on predefined lexical lists of identity terms and word-substitution counterfactuals. This setup introduces an inherent mechanical coupling between the metric (individual unfairness from substituting identity tokens) and the explanation signal (attribution to those exact identity tokens), while potentially missing implicit, indirect, or intersectional biases.

The explanation-based debiasing in RQ3 is only evaluated on encoder-only models (BERT and RoBERTa) due to the computational cost of differentiating through attributions; extending or adapting this to instruction-tuned decoder LLMs is omitted.

The model candidate pool for RQ2 (fair model selection) is relatively small (7 encoder models and 4 decoder configurations), which limits the statistical power of the ranking metrics (Spearman's rank correlation and MRR@1).

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The paper conducts an extensive study covering 14 explanation variants (gradient-, propagation-, perturbation-, and attention-based), multiple model families (encoder-only: BERT, RoBERTa; decoder-only LLMs: Llama 3.2, Qwen3), three bias dimensions (race, gender, religion), and two benchmark datasets.

Well-structured research questions: Decomposing the role of explanations into inference-time detection (RQ1), cross-model validation/selection (RQ2), and training-time mitigation (RQ3) provides a structured and nuanced perspective on where explainability succeeds and fails in promoting fairness.

Honest and actionable insights: Rather than overclaiming, the authors clearly identify negative results (e.g., input-based explanations are unreliable for model selection in RQ2) alongside positive ones (RQ1 and RQ3), offering practical guidelines for practitioners (e.g., preferring L2-norm and Occlusion over mean-based attributions).

Constructive engagement with prior literature: The paper critically examines and contextualizes previous cautionary work (e.g., Dimanov et al., 2020; Pruthi et al., 2020), showing that explanation-based bias detection remains viable when evaluated against fairness metrics and that balanced hyperparameter tuning mitigates performance degradation.

Timely comparison against LLM self-reflection: Comparing post-hoc input explanations with LLM-as-a-judge approaches (self-reflection and self-attribution) provides timely evidence showing that post-hoc explanations still offer superior reliability and calibration over prompt-based self-evaluation.
weaknesses: Reliance on predefined identity lexicons: The sensitive token reliance metric and the counterfactual individual fairness evaluation depend strictly on predefined word lists. In real-world hate speech detection, bias frequently manifests through implicit associations, dialectal markers (e.g., AAE), or coded language without explicit demographic mentions.

Limited algorithmic novelty: The debiasing objective in RQ3 directly adapts existing explanation-regularization formulations (e.g., Dimanov et al., Kennedy et al.). While the comprehensive evaluation and hyperparameter selection strategy are valuable, the core technical contribution is predominantly empirical rather than methodological.

Assumptions of counterfactual substitution: The individual unfairness metric assumes that swapping identity tokens yields valid, semantic-preserving counterfactuals. This perturbation can sometimes result in pragmatically unnatural text or overlook intersectional/contextual nuances.

Visual and presentation density: Several figures (e.g., Figures 1, 2, and 4) pack a substantial amount of information into small bar charts with low readability for individual method labels without zooming in significantly.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study: Evaluates 16 input-based explanation methods across multiple model families (both encoder-only models like BERT/RoBERTa and decoder-only LLMs such as Llama-3.2 and Qwen-3) and two standard benchmarks (Civil Comments, Jigsaw).

Clear and impactful research questions: Systematically organizes the investigation into three core practical dimensions: detecting biased predictions (RQ1), fair model selection (RQ2), and training-time bias mitigation (RQ3).

Valuable negative and nuanced findings: The paper candidly identifies that explanation-based metrics are not reliable for model selection compared to simple validation fairness baselines, and shows that standard explanation faithfulness metrics (e.g., comprehensiveness/sufficiency) do not correlate with a method's fairness auditing utility.

Rigor in addressing adversarial/masking concerns: Carefully analyzes whether explanation-based debiasing conceals bias (Section 5) and benchmarks against LLM-as-a-judge paradigms (Section 6), supported by human auditing studies (Appendix J) and vocabulary coverage ablations (Appendix H).
weaknesses: Reliance on explicit sensitive token lexicons: The methodology hinges on identifying predefined sensitive tokens and measuring attribution on them. In practice, social bias and hate speech nuances frequently manifest implicitly through dialectal markers, syntactic styles, or pragmatic context rather than explicit demographic keywords.

Assumptions behind counterfactual token substitution: The individual unfairness metric assumes that swapping identity tokens should strictly leave model outputs invariant. In real-world hate speech, social context and historical power dynamics mean that identical statements targeting different groups may legitimately differ in severity or toxicity.

Expected baseline advantage in RQ2: The comparison for model selection pits validation-set explanation reliance against validation-set individual unfairness to predict test-set individual unfairness; since individual unfairness on the validation split directly measures the target evaluation metric, it is unsurprising that the baseline substantially outperforms attribution proxies.

Simple prompting setup for LLM judges: The LLM-as-a-judge baseline uses simple zero-shot reflection prompts without exploring structured rationale elicitation or chain-of-thought prompting, which might underestimate LLM capabilities in bias auditing.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical scope: The paper evaluates 16 input-based explanation methods across both encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only LLM architectures (Llama-3.2, Qwen-3 variants) on two standard toxicity/hate speech benchmarks.

Systematic decomposition of the problem: Investigating explainability across three distinct operational stages—instance-level bias auditing (RQ1), cross-model selection (RQ2), and in-training bias mitigation (RQ3)—provides clear and actionable takeaways.

Important negative findings and critical distinction: The paper explicitly shows that while explanations are effective for auditing individual predictions within a single model (RQ1), they fail as reliable metrics for model selection across different model checkpoints or debiasing interventions (RQ2), cautioning practitioners against naive reliance on explanation scores for model ranking.

Extensive supplementary evaluations: The authors include meaningful follow-up analyses, including explanation faithfulness vs. fairness correlation, robustness under incomplete sensitive lexicons, evaluation on sentiment analysis, and a human auditing user study.
weaknesses: Conceptual circularity between Individual Unfairness and sensitive token attribution: Individual unfairness is defined as the change in model prediction when sensitive tokens are counterfactually swapped, while input attribution methods (especially perturbation-based ones like Occlusion) measure the prediction shift when removing or replacing those exact tokens. The high correlation in RQ1 is therefore partly mechanical by construction.

Heavy reliance on predefined identity lexicons: The entire framework rests on identifying explicit sensitive tokens from predetermined word lists. In real-world hate speech, social bias and hate speech frequently operate via implicit stereotypes, African American Vernacular English (AAVE) syntax, coded language, or contextual framing without explicit identity words.

Limited exploration of bias mitigation on decoder-only models: While the paper evaluates decoder-only LLMs in RQ1 and RQ2, RQ3 (explanation-guided training regularization) is restricted to encoder-only models due to computational constraints, leaving open whether explanation-guided fine-tuning scales effectively to generative LLMs.

Limited practical value of RQ2 findings: The baseline of simply computing validation set fairness directly outperforms explanation-based model ranking across all setups while being substantially cheaper computationally, reducing the practical applicability of explanation-based model selection.

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous empirical study evaluating 16 distinct post-hoc explanation variants across both encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa) and decoder-only LLMs (Llama 3.2, Qwen3 variants) on two standard toxicity datasets.

Well-formulated research questions that systematically dissect the utility of explanations across three key operational stages: sample-level bias detection (RQ1), model selection (RQ2), and bias mitigation during training (RQ3).

Provides valuable, nuanced, and actionable takeaways: showing that while input-based explanations are effective for instance-level bias detection and training supervision, they are unreliable for cross-model fairness selection.

Carefully re-examines and qualifies prior literature (e.g., Dimanov et al., 2020) by demonstrating that explanation-based debiasing can succeed when using fairness-balanced tuning, and that certain explanations remain robust bias indicators even after explanation-based debiasing.

Extensive supplementary analyses that significantly strengthen the core findings, including comparisons against LLM-as-a-judge, faithfulness vs. fairness analysis, sensitivity to incomplete token vocabularies, and a user study on human fairness auditing.
weaknesses: There is inherent conceptual coupling between the individual unfairness metric and sensitive token reliance: because individual unfairness is measured via counterfactual replacement of predefined sensitive tokens, perturbation/attribution methods (e.g., Occlusion, gradients) on the exact same token set are almost mechanically predisposed to correlate with prediction changes, which could be discussed more critically.

The motivation for RQ2 (model selection via explanations) is slightly weak from a practical standpoint, as computing validation individual unfairness via counterfactual substitution is computationally cheaper and more direct than generating post-hoc attributions (e.g., KernelSHAP, IntGrad, Occlusion); hence, the negative finding was largely expected.

The primary experiments focus heavily on toxicity/hate speech detection; while Appendix H tests gender bias on sentiment analysis, exploring other tasks (e.g., coreference resolution, text generation) would strengthen the generalizability of the findings across NLP.
Visual presentation in the main body (particularly Figures 2, 3, 4, and 5) is extremely dense, making individual bars and method differences hard to discern without zooming in significantly.
